items.title: Lost Bullet
items.reason: A compact 92-minute French action thriller about a gifted police mechanic framed for murder who must recover ballistic evidence from a missing car. Whole-film criticism from epd Film describes dialogue chiefly bridging one pursuit or gunfight to the next; Metacritic reproduces critics' accounts of a lean structure, practical car destruction and frequent action. Epic Dope offers an important qualification: the action is distributed throughout rather than literally nonstop. Density is therefore assessed as high but not near-continuous, separately from the impact of the biggest crashes. An opening ram-car robbery, a forceful police-station escape, fights, corrupt-officer pursuit and an extended vehicle-heavy climax provide action across different stages of the film. Strengths are tangible vehicle stunts, a physically capable lead and a simple corruption/evidence hook. Weaknesses include implausible police behavior, thin supporting characters, routine dialogue, modest production scale and car-centric repetition. The practical, somewhat classical approach to stunts is not treated as a release-year-based retro score. These DNA values describe content only and do not imply a final match score or publication decision.

items.title: The Roundup
items.reason: A 106-minute Korean crime-action sequel in which detective Ma Seok-do investigates a murderous kidnapper across Vietnam and South Korea. Eye for Film describes an action-dominated narrative with no sustained slowdown once underway, while Asian Movie Pulse specifically reports more frequent and violent action than the preceding film and identifies apartment, lift and bus fights across the runtime. Film-Rezensionen independently describes recurring choreographed fist and knife confrontations, while OutNow emphasizes brisk pacing and a threatening villain. This supports high action density, not an assumption of uninterrupted fighting: extradition, investigation, interrogation and police-team comedy still take screen time. The physically overwhelming lead, close-quarters choreography, a structured car chase and changes of location are strengths. Limits include a predictable criminal plot, a narrow punch-and-knife action palette, routine police brutality played for laughs, and reduced suspense because the protagonist rarely appears endangered. Gunplay is minor, and the police setting is not a military battlefield. Visual craft and retro aesthetic are judged from presentation rather than release year. DNA is descriptive research evidence only, not a final ranking or eligibility conclusion.
